x: The Discussion of the Interpretation of:
In the name of God, Most Gracious, Most Merciful
The Discussion of the Interpretation of His words (2):

God, exalted be His mention and hallowed be His names, instructed His Prophet Muḥammad, may God bless him and grant him peace, by teaching him to put the mention of His most beautiful names before all his actions, and charged him to describe himself with them before all his important concerns. What He instructed and taught him of this He made a custom for all His creation to follow, and a path for them to walk,
in opening the beginnings of their speech and at the heads of their letters, their books, and their needs, so that the significance of what appears in the speaker's words
sufficed for what is hidden of his intent, which is omitted. That is because the bāʾ in
requires a verb to govern it, and no verb is expressed with it. The hearer of the one who says

therefore needs nothing beyond knowing the speaker's intent, without the speaker stating that intent in words, since every speaker who says it at the start of a matter has brought his speech to it, either together with it or before it without separation, something that spares his hearer from needing an explicit indication of what he began his saying with it for.

The hearer's sufficiency with this, without the speaker expressing what is omitted, resembles his sufficiency when he hears someone asked: “What did you eat today?” and he replies: “Food.” He has no need to repeat “I ate” with “food,” because the question put to him about what he ate has already made clear to him that this is the meaning. It is therefore understood that when a speaker says
In the name of God, Most Gracious, Most Merciful
and then begins reciting a surah, his following
In the name of God, Most Gracious, Most Merciful
with the recitation of the surah
In the name of God, Most Gracious, Most Merciful

, and it is understood from it that he means: I recite in the name of God, Most Gracious, Most Merciful. Likewise his saying “In the name of God” when he rises to stand, or sits, or does any of his other actions announces
the meaning he intends by “In the name of God,” and that by his saying “In the name of God” he meant: I stand in the name of God, I sit in the name of God.
And so with all other actions.
What we have said in interpreting this is the meaning of the words of Ibn ʿAbbās, which Abū Kurayb related to us:

c: ʿUthmān b. Saʿīd told us: Bishr b. ʿUmāra told us: Abū Rawq told us, from al-Ḍaḥḥāk, from ʿAbd Allāh b.
m: ʿAbbās, who said: The first thing with which Gabriel came down to Muḥammad, may God bless him and grant him peace, was that he said: O Muḥammad, say: I seek refuge in the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing from Satan the accursed. Then he said: Say: In the name of God, Most Gracious, Most Merciful. He said: Gabriel said to him
: In the name of God, O Muḥammad. He means: Recite with the remembrance of God your Lord, and stand and sit with the remembrance of God.

x: If someone says to us: If the interpretation of God's words
is what you have described, and what governs the bāʾ in
is what you mentioned, how can
be said in the sense of: I recite in the name of God, or: I stand [in the name of God]

, or: I sit in the name of God? You know that everyone who recites the Book of God recites it with God's help and success, and that everyone who stands, sits, or does any deed does so through God, his standing, sitting and deed being by God. And why was it not said, since that is so: “By God, Most Gracious, Most Merciful,” and not
? For the speaker's words “I stand and sit by God, Most Gracious, Most Merciful,” or “I recite by God,” are clearer in meaning to the hearer than “In the name of God,” since the words “I stand,” or
“I sit in the name of God” lead the hearer to suppose that his standing and sitting are by something other than God.
It is said to him, and success is with God: What is intended by that meaning is other than what you imagined to yourself. The meaning of
is rather: I begin with the naming of God and the remembrance of Him before everything; or: I recite by naming Him
; or: I stand and sit by my naming God and remembering Him. [It does not mean]
that he intends by his saying
: I stand by God, or: I recite by God, such that the speaker's words “I recite by God,” or “I stand,” or “I sit by God” would be closer to the correct way than
If the matter is as you describe, how was
said, when you know that ism is a noun, and that tasmiya (naming) is a verbal noun from your saying sammaytu?

The Arabs sometimes produce verbal nouns in varied nouns, without their regular form, as they say: akramtu fulānan karāma. The verbal noun of “afʿaltu,” when brought out on the pattern of its verb, is ifʿāl. Likewise: ahantuhu hawānan, and kallamtuhu kalāman. The verbal noun of “faʿʿaltu” is tafʿīl. Of this is the verse of the poet
: Is it ingratitude after you turned death away from me, and after your gift of the hundred pasturing camels?
He means: iʿṭāʾuka (your giving). And the verse of another
poet: If this miserliness from you is a trait of character, then in my long (ṭūlī) hoping for you I have been an Ashʿab. He means: in
my prolonging (iṭālatī) my hope in you. And the verse of another

, your striking down a man who offered a greeting of salutation is an injustice. He means: iṣābatakum (your striking). Witnesses of this kind are many, and what we have mentioned suffices for one granted the understanding of it. Since
we have described, in that the Arabs frequently bring verbal nouns out on a pattern other than that of their verbs
, and their putting them in the forms of nouns is attested and widespread, the soundness of what we said in interpreting the speaker's words
its meaning, when he begins an action or a saying, is: I begin with the naming of God before my action or before my saying.
Likewise the meaning of the words of one who says, when he begins reciting the Qurʾān,
In the name of God, Most Gracious, Most Merciful

, is: I recite beginning with the naming of God, or: I begin my recitation with the naming of God. So the noun was put in place of the verbal noun of naming, as kalām was put in place of taklīm, and ʿaṭāʾ in place of iʿṭāʾ. The report from ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿAbbās has been transmitted with the same interpretation we have given.

c: Abū Kurayb related to us: ʿUthmān b. Saʿīd told us: Bishr b. ʿUmāra told us: Abū Rawq told us, from al-Ḍaḥḥāk, from ʿAbd Allāh b.
m: ʿAbbās, who said: The first thing with which

Gabriel came down to Muḥammad, may God bless him and grant him peace, was that he said: O Muḥammad, say: I seek refuge in the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing from Satan the accursed. Then he said: Say: In the name of God, Most Gracious, Most Merciful. Ibn ʿAbbās said:

: Gabriel says to him: O Muḥammad, recite with the remembrance of God your Lord, and stand and sit with the remembrance of God. This interpretation from Ibn ʿAbbās announces the soundness of what we said, that what is intended
by the words of one who begins his recitation with
In the name of God, Most Gracious, Most Merciful
is: I recite by naming God and remembering Him, and I begin the recitation by naming God with His most beautiful names and His exalted attributes. It also
makes plain the falsity of the claim of one who asserted that its meaning, from its speaker, is: By God, Most Gracious, Most Merciful, the first

of everything. Moreover, servants were commanded only to begin at the outset of their affairs by naming God, not by reporting His greatness and attributes, like what they were commanded of naming over slaughtered animals and game, at eating and drinking, and in all their actions. So likewise what they were commanded of naming Him at the opening of the recitation of God's revelation, and at the heads of their letters and books. There is no disagreement among all the scholars of the community that if someone, when slaughtering one of the grazing animals, said “By God” and did not say “In the name of God,” he has contravened, by leaving out the saying “In the name of God,” what is prescribed for him at slaughter. It is thus known that he did not mean by “in the name of God”: “by God,” as the claimant said, that the ism of God in the words of God
In the name of God, Most Gracious, Most Merciful

is God; for if it were as he claimed, it would follow that one who says “By God” at slaughtering his sacrifice has said what is prescribed for him to say over the sacrifice. And the consensus of all that one who says this has left what is prescribed for him to say over his sacrifice if he did not say “In the name of God” is clear proof of the falsity of what was claimed of the interpretation of the words “in the name of God,” namely that “by God” is meant by it, and that the name of God is God. This is not a place for lengthy exposition of the name, whether it is the named, or other than it, or an attribute of it, such that we should prolong the book by mentioning it. It is only a place for clarifying the name that is annexed to God, Mighty and Majestic: is it a noun, or a verbal noun meaning naming?

x: What do you say about the verse of Labīd b. Rabīʿa

: Until the year, then the name of peace upon you both; and whoever weeps a full year has made his excuse? One advanced in knowledge of the language of the Arabs has interpreted it as meaning: “then peace upon you both,” and that “the name of peace” is peace

If that were permissible and its interpretation as he interpreted it sound, it would be permissible to say: I saw the name of Zayd, I ate the name of food, I drank the name of drink. The consensus of all the Arabs that this is impossible announces the falsity of the interpretation of one who interpreted Labīd's “then the name of peace upon you both” as meaning “then peace upon you both,” and

of his claim that the insertion of the noun there and its annexation to peace is permissible only because the name of the named is the named itself. Those who hold the view we have related are asked: Do you allow it in Arabic to say “I ate the name of honey,” meaning “I ate honey,” as you permit “ismu l-salāmi ʿalayka”

If they say yes, they have left the language of the Arabs, and have allowed in their language what all the Arabs call an error in their language. If they say no, they are asked for the difference between the two, and whatever they say about one they will be bound to say the same about the other. If someone says to us: What then is the meaning of Labīd's verse in your view?

It admits two interpretations, both different from what the person whose view we related said. One of them: that al-Salām is one of the names of God, so it is possible that Labīd meant by his words “then ismu l-salāmi ʿalaykumā”: then hold fast to the name of God and His remembrance after that, and leave my remembrance and weeping over me, by way of ighrāʾ (urging). He put the noun in the nominative because he placed

the word that carries the sense of urging after it. The Arabs do this when they put the urging word later and put what is urged first, although they may also put it in the accusative while it comes later. Of this is the verse of the poet

I have seen people praising you. He urged with “dūnaka” although it is placed last; the meaning is: dūnaka dalwī (here, take my bucket). So likewise Labīd's words “until the year, then ismu l-salāmi ʿalaykumā” mean: then ʿalaykumā ismu l-salāmi, that is: hold to the remembrance of God, and leave my remembrance and grief for me; for one who has wept a year over a dead man has made his excuse. This is one of its two aspects. The other aspect is: then my naming of God over you both. This is as one says of something he sees that pleases him: “ismu llāhi ʿalayka” (the name of God be upon you), warding off evil from it by that; it is as if he said: then the name of God be upon you both against evil. The first aspect resembles Labīd's meaning more closely of the two. And it is said to the one who directs Labīd's verse to the meaning “then peace upon you both”: Do you consider what we said in these two aspects permissible, or one of them, or something other than what you said about it?

If he says: No, he shows the extent of his knowledge of the varied usages of Arab speech, and spares his opponent from debating him. If he says: Yes, it is said to him: What is your proof that what you claimed of the interpretation is the correct one, rather than what I said it admits, such that we are obliged to concede it to you? There is no way to that.

c: As for the report that Ismāʿīl b. al-Faḍl related to us:
m: Ibrāhīm b. al-ʿAlāʾ b. al-Ḍaḥḥāk [who is nicknamed Zibrīq]

told us: Ismāʿīl b. ʿAyyāsh told us, from Ismāʿīl b. Yaḥyā, from Ibn Abī Mulayka, from one who related it to him, from Ibn Masʿūd, and Misʿar b. Kidām, from ʿAṭiyya, from Abū Saʿīd, who said: The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: “Jesus son of Mary was handed over by his mother to the kuttāb (school) to be taught. The teacher said to him: Write: bi-smi. Jesus said to him: What is bi-smi? The teacher said: I do not know. Jesus said to him
: The bāʾ is the splendour of God (bahāʾ), the sīn is His radiance (sanāʾ), and the mīm is His dominion (mamlaka)”
. I fear that this is an error on the part of the transmitter, and that he meant [b-s-m] in the way beginners among the children are taught, in the kuttāb, the letters of [abjad]
, and erred by joining them, so that he said bi-smi. For this interpretation has no meaning when
In the name of God, Most Gracious, Most Merciful

is recited as the reciter recites it in the Book of God Almighty, since its meaning, if its interpretation is carried to that, departs from what is understood by it among all the Arabs and the people of their language.

x: The Discussion of the Interpretation of the words of God, majestic is His praise and hallowed be His names:
As for the interpretation of God's words
, it accords with what has been reported to us from ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿAbbās: He is the One whom everything worships (yaʾlahuhu)

c: This is because Abū Kurayb related to us: ʿUthmān b. Saʿīd told us: Bishr b. ʿUmāra told us: Abū Rawq told us, from al-Ḍaḥḥāk, from ʿAbd Allāh b.
m: ʿAbbās, who said: God is the One who holds divinity and the right to servanthood over all His creation

x: Does this have a base in the pattern “faʿala yafʿalu,” from which this name was formed
Not by hearing from the Arabs, but by inference.
What shows that ulūhiyya is worship, that ilāh is the one worshipped, and that it has a base in “faʿala yafʿalu”?
There is no dispute among the Arabs in judging as correct, without disagreement, the saying of one who describes a man devoted to worship and seeking what
is with God, mighty is His mention: taʾallaha fulān.

i: Of this is the verse of Ruʾba b. al-ʿAjjāj
x: How excellent are the fair women, the praisers
, they glorified God and said “We belong to God” at my devotion (taʾalluhī).

He means: at my worship and my seeking God by my deed. There is no doubt that taʾalluh, of the pattern tafaʿʿul, is from alaha yaʾlahu, and that the meaning of alaha, when it is uttered, is: he worshipped God. A verbal noun of it has also come that shows that the Arabs have used from it the pattern “faʿila yafʿalu” without augmentation.

c: That is what Sufyān b. Wakīʿ related to us: My father told us, from Nāfiʿ b.
m: ʿUmar, from ʿAmr b. Dīnār, from Ibn ʿAbbās, that he recited: (wa-yadharaka wa-ilāhataka)
. He said: Your worship. He said: He was worshipped and did not worship

c: And Sufyān related to us: Ibn ʿUyayna told us, from ʿAmr b.
m: Dīnār, from Muḥammad b. ʿAmr b. al-Ḥasan, from Ibn ʿAbbās: (wa-yadharaka wa-ilāhataka). He said: Pharaoh was worshipped and did not worship. [Ibn ʿAbbās
and Mujāhid recited it so too]

c: And al-Qāsim related to us:
m: told us: Ḥajjāj related to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujāhid, concerning his reading (wa-yadharaka wa-ilāhataka). He said: and your worship. There is no doubt that al-ilāha

, as Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid explained it, is a verbal noun from the saying: alaha fulānun Allāha ilāhatan, as one says: ʿabada fulānun Allāha ʿibādatan, and ʿabara al-ruʾyā ʿibāratan. So this statement of Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid shows that alaha means ʿabada (he worshipped), and that ilāha is its verbal noun.

x: If it is allowable to say of one who worshipped God: alahahu, on the interpretation of Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid, how should it be said when the reporter wishes [to report]
God's rightful claim to that over His servant?
As for transmission, we have no transmission on it
, but what is required follows the analogy of what came in the report from the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, which Ismāʿīl b. al-Faḍl related to us:

c: Ibrāhīm b. al-ʿAlāʾ told us: Ismāʿīl b. ʿAyyāsh told us, from Ismāʿīl b.
m: Yaḥyā, from Ibn Abī Mulayka, from one who related it to him, from Ibn Masʿūd, and Misʿar b. Kidām, from ʿAṭiyya al-ʿAwfī, from Abū Saʿīd, who said: The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: “Jesus was handed over by his mother to the kuttāb to be taught. The teacher said to him: Write: Allāh. Jesus said to him: Do you know what Allāh is? Allāh is the God of the gods (ilāh al-ālihah)” — that it be said: God, majestic is His praise, is the god of the servant, and the servant is the one who worships Him (alahahu). And that the saying of the speaker “Allāh” belongs to the kind of speech

x: How can that be so, given the difference between their two forms
Just as it can be that His words
But as for me, He is God, my Lord
[al-Kahf 18:38] have as their origin: lākin anā, huwa Allāhu rabbī. As the poet says
: You shoot me with a glance, as if to say that you are the one wronged, and you hate me, but as for me (lākinnā), I do not hate you

. He means: lākin anā, I do not hate you. He dropped the hamza of anā, so the nūn of anā met the nūn of lākin, which is unvowelled, and it was assimilated into the nūn of anā, and the two became one doubled nūn. Likewise Allāh: its origin is al-ilāh.

The hamza, which is the fāʾ of the noun, was dropped, so the lām which is the ʿayn of the noun met the additional lām that entered with the additional alif, which is unvowelled, and it was assimilated into the other, which is the ʿayn of the noun, and the two became in pronunciation a single doubled lām, as we described regarding God's words:
But as for me, He is God, my Lord

evidence.text: [Ibn ʿAbbās (4) and Mujāhid recited it so too] (5).
And al-Qāsim related to us: [al-Ḥusayn b. Dāwūd] (6) told us: Ḥajjāj related to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujāhid, concerning his reading (wa-yadharaka wa-ilāhataka).

x: The Discussion of the Interpretation of His words, Exalted:
, it is of the pattern faʿlān, from raḥima

is of the pattern faʿīl from it. The Arabs often build nouns from “faʿila yafʿalu” on faʿlān, as they say from ghaḍiba: ghaḍbān; from sakira: sakrān; and from ʿaṭisha: ʿaṭshān. Likewise their saying raḥmān from raḥima, because its “faʿila” form
is raḥima yarḥamu. And raḥīm was said, even though the ʿayn of its “faʿila” form

is vowelled with kasra, because it is praise, and it is the custom of the Arabs to carry noun patterns, when they contain praise or blame, onto faʿīl, whether the ʿayn of the verb form is vowelled with kasra or with fatḥa, as they said from ʿalima: ʿālim and ʿalīm; and from qadara: qādir and qadīr. That is not a building of those on the pattern of their verbs, because the pattern from “faʿila yafʿalu” and “faʿala yafʿilu” is fāʿil; had al-raḥmān and al-raḥīm come out on
the pattern of their verbs, their form would have been al-rāḥim.
Since al-raḥmān and al-raḥīm are two names derived from raḥma (mercy), what is the point of repeating them, when one of them conveys the meaning of the other?
you supposed; each of the two words has a meaning that the other does not convey.
What is the meaning in which each is distinct, so that one does not convey the meaning of the other?

As for the Arabic-language aspect, there is no dispute among those who know the languages of the Arabs that the saying al-raḥmān departs further from the noun patterns of “faʿila yafʿalu” than the saying al-raḥīm; and there is no disagreement among them that every noun that has a base in “faʿila yafʿalu” and then departs further from its base of “faʿila yafʿalu,” the one described by it is preferred over the one described by the noun built on its base of “faʿula yafʿulu,” when the naming is by way of praise or blame. So this is what the saying al-raḥmān contains of additional meaning over the saying al-raḥīm, in language. As for the aspect of report and tradition, the interpreters differ

c: Al-Sarī b. Yaḥyā al-Tamīmī related to me: ʿUthmān b. Zufar told us:
m: : He said: al-Raḥmān is to all creation, al-Raḥīm, he said, to the believers

c: Ismāʿīl b. al-Faḍl related to us: Ibrāhīm b. al-ʿAlāʾ told us: Ismāʿīl b. ʿAyyāsh told us, from Ismāʿīl b.
m: Yaḥyā, from Ibn Abī Mulayka, from one who related it to him, from Ibn Masʿūd, and Misʿar b. Kidām, from ʿAṭiyya al-ʿAwfī, from Abū Saʿīd, who said: The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: “Jesus son of Mary said: al-Raḥmān is the Most Gracious of the Hereafter and this world, and al-Raḥīm is the Most Merciful of the Hereafter.” These two reports announce the difference between God's, majestic is His praise, naming with His name that is raḥmān and His naming with His name that is raḥīm, and the difference in the meaning
of the two words, even if they differ in the meaning of that difference, so that one of them shows that this is in this world, and the other shows that it is in the Hereafter.

x: Which of these two interpretations is more correct in your view?

Each of them has in our view a sound way out, so there is no ground for asking which of the two is more correct. That is because the meaning in naming God al-Raḥmān, as distinct from the meaning in naming Him al-Raḥīm, is that by the name al-Raḥmān He is described as having mercy that extends to all His creation, and by the name [al-Raḥīm He is described]

as having mercy specific to some of His creation, whether in all circumstances or in some. There is no doubt, then, that the specificity in describing Him as al-Raḥīm does not change its meaning, whether in this world, in the Hereafter, or in both. Since what we have said is sound, and God, majestic is His praise, has singled out His believing servants in this present world with the gracious favour He showed

them in granting them success in obeying Him, in believing in Him and in His messengers, in following His command and avoiding His acts of disobedience, from which He withheld help from the one who associated partners with Him, disbelieved, opposed what he was commanded, and committed acts of disobedience against Him; and since He, majestic is His praise, has also made what He has prepared for those who believe in Him in the future abode in His gardens, the lasting bliss and the manifest triumph, a part of His mercy in this world and the Hereafter, alongside what He has extended to them and to the unbelievers in this world, of bounty and kindness to all of them, in the expansion of provision, the subjection of the clouds to bring rain, the bringing forth of plants from the earth, the soundness of bodies and minds, and the other countless blessings in which believers and unbelievers share, our Lord, majestic is His praise, is the Most Gracious of all His creation in this world and the Hereafter, and the Most Merciful of the believers in particular, in this world and the Hereafter. As for the mercy with which He encompassed all of them in this world, by which He is raḥmān
to them, it is what we have mentioned together with its counterparts, which none of His creatures can count, as He, majestic is His praise, said:
If you count God's blessing, you will not be able to enumerate it
As for the Hereafter, the mercy with which He encompassed all of them there, by which He is Most Gracious to them, lies
in His treating all of them equally, majestic is His mention, in His justice and judgement, so that He wrongs none of them by the weight of an atom, and if there is a good deed He multiplies it

, and gives each soul in full what it has earned. That is the meaning of His general mercy over all of them in the Hereafter, by which He is Most Gracious in the Hereafter. As for what He specified for the believers in this present world of His mercy, by which He is Most Merciful to them in it, as He, majestic is His mention, said:
And He is ever Merciful to the believers

[al-Aḥzāb 33:43], it is the gracious favour in their religion that we described, which He granted to them and withheld from those of the unbelievers whom He abandoned. As for what He specified for them in the Hereafter, by which He is Most Merciful to them and not to the unbelievers, it is what we described above
of the bliss and honour, beyond what hopes can reach, that He prepared for them and not for others.

c: The other view on its interpretation is what Abū Kurayb related to us: ʿUthmān b. Saʿīd told us: Bishr b. ʿUmāra told us: Abū Rawq told us, from al-Ḍaḥḥāk, from ʿAbd Allāh b.
m: is the faʿlān form from raḥma (mercy), and it belongs to the speech of the Arabs. He said:

The third view on the interpretation of this is what ʿImrān b. Bakkār al-Kalāʿī related to me:

c: Yaḥyā b. Ṣāliḥ told us:
m: Abū al-Azhar Naṣr b. ʿAmr al-Lakhmī, of the people of Palestine, told us: I heard ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī say: It was “al-Raḥmān”; when al-Raḥmān was cut away (ukhtuzila) from His name, it became “al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm”

. What ʿAṭāʾ meant by this, God willing, is that al-Raḥmān was one of the names of God by which none of His creatures was named; when the liar Musaylima named himself by it, and that is his “cutting away” of it, meaning his taking it from God's names for himself, God, majestic is His praise, announced that His name is al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm; so that by this He would distinguish for His servants His name from the name of those who had taken His names for themselves, since no one other than Him, majestic is His mention, is named al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm, such that these two names are joined for him. Some of His creatures are named

either Raḥīm or Raḥmān, but Raḥmān Raḥīm has never been joined for anyone but Him, and the two are not joined for anyone besides Him. So the meaning of this saying of ʿAṭāʾ is that God, majestic is His praise, distinguished His name from the name of any other of His creatures by following al-Raḥmān with al-Raḥīm, whether the two differ in meaning or agree. What ʿAṭāʾ said is sound in meaning; it is rather possible that He, majestic is His praise, reserved for Himself being named with both together, to set it apart from His creatures, in order to make His servants know, by the mention of the two together, that He alone is intended by their mention, to the exclusion of anyone else among His creatures, along with the meaning in the interpretation of each of them that the other lacks.

x: Some of the dull-witted have claimed that the Arabs did not know al-Raḥmān and that it was not in
their language, and that for this reason the polytheists said to the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace:
And what is the Raḥmān? Shall we prostrate to what you command us?
[al-Furqān 25:60], in denial of this name. In his view it was as if
it were impossible that polytheists deny what they knew to be true, or
as if he had not recited from the Book of God the words of God:
Those to whom We gave the Book know him
(meaning Muḥammad, may God bless him and grant him peace)
as they know their own sons

[al-Baqara 2:146]. Yet they were at the same time rejecting him and denying his prophethood. So it is known from this that they used to dispute the reality of what had been established as sound with them and what they knew with certainty. A verse has also been recited from one of the ignorant of the Jāhiliyya
: Behold, that [girl has struck her hajīn]
/ Behold, may al-Raḥmān, my Lord, cut off her right hand.
And Salāma b. Jandal al-Saʿdī said
: You rushed upon us, our two rushes

upon you; and whatever al-Raḥmān wills, He binds and looses. Some who have weak knowledge of the interpretation of the exegetes, and little transmission of the sayings of the early authorities among the commentators

, have also claimed that the figurative sense (majāz) of al-Raḥmān is “possessor of mercy,” and of al-Raḥīm is “the one who shows mercy.” Then he said: They sometimes derive the two words from one word with the meaning being one, owing to the breadth of speech among them. He said: They did the same in saying nadmān and nadīm. Then he cited as witness [the verse of Burj]
b. Mushir al-Ṭāʾī: Many a drinking companion (nadmān) who makes the cup sweeter, I served him when the stars had set

. And he cited verses similar to it concerning nadīm and nadmān. He thus distinguished between the meaning of al-Raḥmān and al-Raḥīm in the interpretation, in saying: al-Raḥmān is the possessor of mercy, and al-Raḥīm is the one who shows mercy; although he left aside explaining the interpretation of their two meanings
on its soundness, and then illustrated
this with two words [that come with one meaning], so he returned to what he had made two meanings and made it an example of what has a single meaning, despite the difference of the words.

There is no doubt that the possessor of mercy is the one for whom mercy has been established and for whom it is sound that it is an attribute, and that the one who shows mercy is described as one who will show mercy, or has shown mercy and that act is complete, or is in the midst of it; and in that there is then no indication

that mercy is an attribute of his, as there is an indication that it is his attribute when he is described as possessor of mercy. So where is the meaning of al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm, on his interpretation, in relation to the meaning of two words derived from a single word, with differing wording and the same meanings? But a statement that has no firm foundation to rely on has its flaw plain to see.
Why did He put His name Allāh before His name al-Raḥmān, and His name al-Raḥmān before His name al-Raḥīm?

Because it is the habit of the Arabs, when they wish to report about one who is reported on, to put his name first and then to follow it with his attributes and epithets; and this is what is required by rule, that the name be placed before its epithet and attribute, so that the hearer knows about whom the report is. Since that is so, and God, majestic is His mention, has names that He forbade His creatures to be named by, reserving them to Himself apart from them, such as Allāh, al-Raḥmān and al-Khāliq, and names that He permitted them to use of one another, such as al-Raḥīm, al-Samīʿ, al-Baṣīr, al-Karīm and similar names, it was required that His names that belong to Him alone, apart from all His creation, come first, so that the hearer knows to whom the praise and glorification are directed; and that these be followed by His names by which others also are named, after the one addressed or the hearer knows to whom what follows of the meanings is directed. So God, majestic is His mention, began with His name Allāh, because divinity belongs to none other than Him, majestic is His praise, in any respect, neither by way of being named by it nor by way of meaning. For we have shown that the meaning of “Allāh,” majestic is His praise, is the meaning
of the one worshipped, and there is no one worshipped but Him, majestic is His praise; and that God has forbidden being named by it, even if the one who takes the name intends what
the one named Saʿīd (happy) intends while he is wretched, or the one named Ḥasan (handsome) while he is ugly.
Do you not see that God, majestic is His praise, said in more than one verse of His Book:
Is there a god with God?
[al-Naml 27:60, 61, 62, 63, 64]? He thus regarded it as monstrous in one who professes it. And He, Exalted, said, in singling Himself out
Say: Call upon God or call upon the Raḥmān; whichever you call upon, to Him belong the most beautiful names

with His name al-Raḥmān, since He had also forbidden His creation to be named by it, although some of His creatures may deserve to be named by some of its meanings. That is because it is permissible to describe many of those below God among His creatures with some attributes of mercy, whereas it is impermissible for anyone beside Him to deserve any part of divinity; so for that reason al-Raḥmān came second

to His name Allāh. As for His name al-Raḥīm, we have mentioned that it is among the names by which it is permissible to describe others, and mercy is among His attributes, majestic is His mention; so, the matter being as we described, it fell into the positions of epithets of names, which follow
them after the names have come first.

This is the reason for putting His name Allāh before His name al-Raḥmān, and His name al-Raḥmān before His name al-Raḥīm. Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī also said of al-Raḥmān what we have said, that it is among the names of God by which servants were forbidden to be named.

m: , from al-Ḥasan, who said: al-Raḥmān is a prohibited name

x: There is no dispute among those who know the languages of the Arabs in judging as correct the saying “Praise be to God, in thanks” (al-ḥamdu lillāhi shukran). It is thus evident
, since this is sound among all of them

can be uttered in the place of thanks, and thanks can be put in the place of praise; for if that were not so, it would not be permissible to say: “Praise be to God, in thanks.” It would be excluded from the speaker's words: “Praise be to God” as a verbal noun of “I thank” (ashkuru); for if shukr did not have the meaning of ḥamd, it would be an error to derive from ḥamd a verbal noun other
than its meaning and other than its wording
What is the reason for the entry of alif and lām into al-ḥamd? Why was it not said: ḥamdan lillāhi rabbi l-ʿālamīn?
The entry of alif and lām into al-ḥamd has a meaning that the speaker's “ḥamdan lillāh”
, without alif and lām, does not convey. That is because their entry into al-ḥamd [announces]

that its meaning is: all praises and complete thanks belong to God. Had the two been dropped, it would indicate only that the speaker's praise belongs to God to the exclusion of all praises, since the meaning of the speaker's “ḥamdan lillāh,” or [“ḥamdun lillāh”]
, is: I praise God with praise. But the interpretation of the speaker's
Praise be to God, Lord of the Worlds

when reciting Sūrat Umm al-Qurʾān is not “I praise God”; the interpretation is rather what we described before, that all praises belong to God by virtue of His divinity and His bestowal on His creation of the blessings He bestowed on them, which have no equal
in religion and this world, the present and the future. For this reason the reading of the reciters and scholars of the community has been continuous in the nominative for al-ḥamd in
Praise be to God, Lord of the Worlds
, rather than the accusative, which would indicate that the meaning of the one who recites it so is: I praise God with praise.
Were a reciter to recite it with the accusative
, in my view he would distort its meaning, and deserve punishment for reciting it so, if he deliberately recites it so while knowing its error and the corruption of its interpretation.
What is the meaning of His words

? Did God praise Himself, majestic is His praise, and extol Himself, and then teach it to us so that we say it as He said it and described Himself with it? If that is so, what is the reason for His words, Exalted is His mention,
You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help
, when He, mighty is His mention, is the one worshipped and not a worshipper? Or
of Gabriel, or of Muḥammad, the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace? In that case it would be void for this to be God's speech.
Rather, all of this is the speech of God, majestic is His praise; but He, majestic is His mention, praised Himself and extolled Himself with what He is [deserving of]
, then taught that to His servants and made its recitation obligatory for them, as a test and trial from Him of them. So He said to them: Say:
Praise be to God, Lord of the Worlds
You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help
are among what He, majestic is His mention, taught them to say and to profess in its meaning, and this is joined to His words
Praise be to God, Lord of the Worlds
; it is as if He said: Say this, and this.
Where are His words “Say,” such that the interpretation of this would be what you claimed?
We have shown in what preceded that
it is the habit of the Arabs, when they know the place of the word and do not doubt

that its hearer knows from what they voiced of their speech what they omitted, to omit what is rendered unnecessary by the apparent part of their speech, particularly if the omitted word is a saying or has the sense
of a saying, as the poet said
: And I know that I shall become a grave
set out and he does not set out / The askers
He means by this: and the informers
said to them: The dead man is Wazīr. So he dropped “the dead man,” since he had said what indicates it. Likewise the words of another
: [And you saw your husband in the battle]
, having slung on a sword and a spear He knew that a spear is not slung on, [and that he only]

meant: and carrying a spear. But since the meaning was known, he relied on what appeared of his speech instead of expressing what he omitted from it. They also say to the traveller when they bid him farewell: “Accompanied, in good health!” [By this is meant: Travel accompanied, in good health! And they omit]
“travel” and “set out”, because its meaning is known even if its mention is dropped. Likewise what was omitted from God's words, Exalted is His mention:
Praise be to God, Lord of the Worlds
: since His words, majestic is His mention,
made known what He meant by
Praise be to God, Lord of the Worlds
of the sense of His command to His servants, the indication of what appeared of the saying made it unnecessary to state what was omitted.
We have also related the report
we mentioned at the outset, in the interpretation
Praise be to God, Lord of the Worlds
, from Ibn ʿAbbās, that he used to say: Gabriel said to Muḥammad: Say, O Muḥammad:
Praise be to God, Lord of the Worlds

. And we showed that Gabriel only taught Muḥammad, may God bless him and grant him peace, what he was commanded to teach him, and this report announces the soundness of what we said in the interpretation of that

The explanation of the interpretation of God's name Allāh, in
, has already been given, so there is no need for us to repeat it in this place
. As for the interpretation of His words
: in the speech of the Arabs, rabb has several meanings
. The master who is obeyed among them
is called rabb. Of this is the verse of Labīd b. Rabīʿa
: And they destroyed one day the rabb of Kinda and his son, and the rabb of Maʿadd, between Khabt
. By “the rabb of Kinda” he means: the master of Kinda. And of this is the verse of al-Nābigha of Banū Dhubyān
: She hastens to al-Nuʿmān until she reaches him; [a ransom for you]
wealth, from a rabb. And the man who sets a thing right is called a rabb
. Of this is the verse of al-Farazdaq b. Ghālib
: They were like a foolish ghee-maker who, when she stored her ghee
, stored it in a hide that had not been cured (marbūb).
By this he means: in a hide that had not been set right (muṣlaḥ).
so-and-so “yarubbu ṣanīʿatahu” with so-and-so, when he tries to set it right and make it last. Of this is the verse of ʿAlqama b. ʿAbada
a man to whom the charge of me (ribābatī)
took charge of me, and I went to ruin.
By his words afḍat ilayka he means: my ribāba
reached you, and you became the one who takes charge (tarubbu) of my affair and sets it right, when I left the ribāba of others among the kings

who were over me before you, who neglected my affair and left off looking after it. They are the rubūb, of which the singular is rabb; and the owner of a thing is called its rabb. The meaning of rabb also varies in other respects, but these return to one of these three aspects. So our Lord, majestic is His praise, is the master who has no peer
and no like in the like
of His sovereignty; the one who sets right the affairs of His creation with the blessings He has lavished on them; and the owner to whom belong creation and command. A report [similar to what]
we said in the interpretation of His words, majestic is His praise,

x: The Discussion of the Interpretation of His words, Mighty and Majestic:
The explanation of the interpretation of His words
has already been given in the interpretation of
In the name of God, Most Gracious, Most Merciful
, which makes repeating it in this place unnecessary
. We also did not need to explain the reason for the repetition
of that in this place, since we do not regard
In the name of God, Most Gracious, Most Merciful

as a verse of the Opening of the Book, such that a questioner could press on us the question: What is the reason for repeating this in this place, when God, majestic is His praise, has already described Himself with it in His words
In the name of God, Most Gracious, Most Merciful
, with one of the two verses near the other and adjacent to its companion? Rather, this is for us an argument against the error of the claim of one who claimed that
In the name of God, Most Gracious, Most Merciful
is a verse of the Opening of the Book; for if it were so, it would be the repetition of a verse with one meaning and one wording twice, with no separator

And in nothing of the Book of God are there two adjacent verses repeated with one wording and one meaning, with no separation between them by speech whose meaning differs from their meaning. A verse is repeated in its entirety in a single surah only with separations between the repetitions, and interposed speech with a meaning other than that of the repeated verses or with different wording; and there is no separator between
In the name of God, Most Gracious, Most Merciful
Praise be to God, Lord of the Worlds
Praise be to God, Lord of the Worlds

is a separator between (2) them. It is said: A group of the interpreters denied this, and said: This belongs to the postponed that has the sense of being advanced, and the text is rather: Praise be to God, Most Gracious, Most Merciful, Lord of the Worlds, Master of the Day of Judgement. They cited as evidence for the soundness of what they claimed His words: (Malik of the Day of Judgement). They said: His words (Malik of the Day of Judgement) are God's teaching His servant to describe Him as King (malik) in the reading of one who reads (Malik), and as owner (mālik, possessing milk) in the reading of one who reads
. They said: What is more fitting to be placed next to His description as sovereignty (mulk) or ownership (milk) is a description of the same kind, and that is His words:

, which is a report of His ownership of all classes of creation; and what is next to His description with greatness and divinity should be what is its like in meaning, of praise of Him, and that is His words
They claimed that this is for them evidence that His words
have the sense of coming before
, although apparently placed after. And they

said: Instances of this, of advancing that has the sense of postponing and postponing that has the sense of advancing, are more widespread in the speech of the Arabs and more numerous in their utterance than can be counted. Of this is the verse of Jarīr b. ʿAṭiyya
: The phantom visited, and how remote from you is a brief visit (limām)
! Return to your visitor a greeting for his greeting. It means: the phantom visited briefly (limāman), and how far is it from you? And as He, majestic is His praise, said in His mighty Book:
Praise be to God, who sent down to His servant the Book and made not in it any crookedness
[al-Kahf 18:1], with the sense: Praise be to God who sent down to His servant the Book straight and made not in it any crookedness; and the like.
In that is evidence attesting to the soundness of the statement of those who denied that
In the name of God, Most Gracious, Most Merciful
is a verse of the Opening of the Book.

evidence.text: They said: His words (Malik of the Day of Judgement) are God's teaching His servant to describe Him as King (malik) in the reading of one who reads (Malik), and as owner (mālik, possessing milk) in the reading of one who reads {Mālik}.

x: The Discussion of the Interpretation of His words:
Mālik of the Day of Judgement
The reciters differ in the recitation of
Mālik of the Day of Judgement
. Some recite it (Malik of the Day of Judgement), some recite it
Mālik of the Day of Judgement
, and some recite it (Mālika yawmi l-dīn), with fatḥa on the kāf

. We have given an exhaustive account of the transmission from those from whom a reading on this has been reported, in the book “al-Qirāʾāt”, and informed of the reading we choose on it and the reason that makes what we chose of the reading sound; so we disliked repeating it in this place, since what we intend in this book of ours is the explanation of the interpretations of the verses of the Qurʾān, not of the modes of their recitation. There is no disagreement among all who know the languages of the Arabs that malik (king) is derived from mulk (sovereignty), and that mālik (owner) is taken from milk (ownership). The interpretation of the reading of one who reads (Malik of the Day of Judgement) is that sovereignty belongs purely to God on the Day of Judgement, to the exclusion of all His creation who were before that in the world tyrant kings contending with Him for sovereignty and disputing His sole possession of pride, greatness, authority, and might; and so they became certain
, by meeting God on the Day of Judgement, that they were the small and abased, and that to Him, apart
from them and from others, belong sovereignty, pride, might and splendour, as He, majestic is His mention and hallowed be His names, said in His revelation:
On the day when they come forth, nothing of them hidden from God: To whom belongs sovereignty this day? To God, the One, the Subduer

So He, Exalted, announced that He alone possesses sovereignty on that day, to the exclusion of the kings of the world, who on the Day of Judgement pass from their sovereignty to abasement and smallness, and from their worldly life to loss in the return.
As for the interpretation of the reading of one who reads
Mālik of the Day of Judgement
, it is what Abū Kurayb related to us:

c: ʿUthmān b. Saʿīd told us, from Bishr b.
m: ʿUmāra: Abū Rawq told us, from al-Ḍaḥḥāk, from Ibn ʿAbbās:
Mālik of the Day of Judgement
. He says: No one on that day will have with Him authority, like their ownership in the world. Then He said:
They will not speak, except for him whom the Most Gracious permits and who speaks what is right
And the voices will be humbled before the Most Gracious
And they do not intercede except for those He approves of

x: Of the two interpretations, the more fitting for the verse, and of the two readings, the sounder in recitation in my view, is the first interpretation and

the reading of one who reads (Malik), in the sense of sovereignty; because in acknowledging His sole possession of sovereignty is a necessary affirmation of His sole possession of ownership, together with the excellence of the surplus of malik over mālik
, since it is known that there is no king who is not an owner, while an owner may not be a king. Furthermore, God, majestic is His mention, has informed His servants in the verse before His words
Mālik of the Day of Judgement
that He is the owner of all the worlds, their master, the one who sets them right, [the one who looks after them]
, and the Most Merciful to them in this world and the Hereafter, in His words
Lord of the Worlds (2) Most Gracious, Most Merciful
He, majestic is His mention, had informed them of His ownership of them in this way by His words
, the most fitting of His attributes to follow that is the one that His words
Lord of the Worlds (2) Most Gracious, Most Merciful
did not contain, given the nearness of the two verses in continuity and adjacency, since His wisdom is the wisdom that no wisdom resembles. And in repeating His description as
Mālik of the Day of Judgement
there would be a repeating of what had already preceded of His description with it in His words

, with the two verses close together and the two attributes adjacent; and there would be in repeating this a repetition of different wordings with the same meanings, which gives a hearer of what is repeated no benefit that he needs. And that which His, majestic is His mention of His attributes, preceding His words
Mālik of the Day of Judgement
, lacks is the meaning in His words (Malik of the Day of Judgement), and that is His description as the King.

It is evident then that the sounder of the two readings and the more deserving of the two interpretations of the Book is the reading of one who reads (Malik of the Day of Judgement), in the sense of sovereignty belonging purely to Him on the Day of Judgement, rather than the reading of one who reads
Mālik of the Day of Judgement
that He owns judgement between them and the decision of the verdict, alone in it among all His creation. If someone supposes that His words
Praise be to God, Lord of the Worlds
are a report of His ownership of them in this world and not the Hereafter, so that it was necessary
with the report from Himself that He
owns them in the Hereafter as He owns them in this world, by His words
Mālik of the Day of Judgement
and supposed wrongly. For if it were permissible for someone to suppose that His words
are restricted in their meaning to the report of His lordship

over the world of this life and not the world of the Hereafter, with no indication that the meaning is so, in the apparent text of the revelation, or in a report transmitted from the Messenger, may God bless him and grant him peace, or in an argument found in reason, it would be permissible
for another to suppose that it is restricted to the world of the time in which
was sent down, to the exclusion of all the worlds that come into being after it in subsequent times; since it is sound, by what we presented earlier
in explanation, that the world of every time is other than the world of the time that follows it.
And if someone of dull understanding is heedless of knowing the soundness of this by what we presented, then in the words of God, majestic is His praise:
And We gave the Children of Israel the Book, and judgement, and prophethood, and provided them with good things, and preferred them over the worlds

[al-Jāthiya 45:16], there is a clear indication that the world of every time is other than the world of the time that was before it and the world of the time that comes after it, since God, majestic is His praise, preferred the community of our Prophet Muḥammad, may God bless him and grant him peace, over all the past communities, and told them of this in His words:
You are the best community brought forth for mankind

[Āl ʿImrān 3:110], the verse. It is thus known that the Children of Israel in the age of our Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, were not, while denying him, the best of the worlds; rather the best of the worlds in that age and after it until the Hour were the believers in him who followed his way, to the exclusion of the other communities that denied him and strayed from his way.
Since the falsity of the interpretation of an interpreter who would interpret His words

as meaning that God is the Lord of the worlds of the time of our Prophet Muḥammad, may God bless him and grant him peace, to the exclusion of the worlds of all other times, is evident, the falsity of the statement of one who claimed that its interpretation is: Lord of the world of this life, not the world of the Hereafter, is also evident; and likewise that
Mālik of the Day of Judgement

deserved to be joined to it, so that it be known that in the Hereafter He has the same ownership and lordship over them as He had in this world. The one who claims this is asked for the difference between him and an arbitrary person like him in the interpretation of His words
: He meant only that He is the Lord of the worlds of the time of Muḥammad, to the exclusion of the worlds of other times, past before him and coming after him, like what the author
of this statement asserts that He [meant by it the worlds of]
this life to the exclusion of the worlds
of the Hereafter, in terms of a basis or an indication.
He will say nothing about one of the two without being held to the same about the other. As for one who claims that the interpretation of His words
Mālik of the Day of Judgement

is that He is the one who has power to establish the Day of Judgement, what we pressed on the author of the preceding statement applies equally to him, since the establishing of the resurrection is the restoration of the creatures who have perished to their forms in which they were before destruction, in the abode
prepared for them what He prepared; and they are the worlds of whom He, majestic is His mention, informed that He is their Lord in His words
. As for the interpretation of this in the reading of one who reads (Mālika yawmi l-dīn), he meant: O
Mālika of the Day of Judgement. He put it in the accusative with the intent of vocative and invocation, as He, majestic is His praise, said:
[Yūsuf 12:29], with the sense: O Yūsuf, turn away from this.
And as the poet of Banū Asad said, which is a verse, it is said, of the Jāhiliyya
of it falsely, Jazʾ, then may you meet its like quickly. He means: Yā Jazʾ (O Jazʾ). And as another said
: You lie, by the House of God, you will not marry her, O sons of the one whose two braids
have turned grey, who ties the udder
sons of the one whose two braids have turned grey. What led him into reading this with the accusative of the kāf of (Mālika), in the sense I described, was his confusion over how to direct His words
You alone we worship and You alone we ask for help
Mālik of the Day of Judgement
. He supposed that its meaning would not be sound after the genitive
Mālik of the Day of Judgement
, so he put it in the accusative, (Mālika yawmi l-dīn), so that
would be an address to Him, as if he meant: O Mālik of the Day of Judgement, You alone we worship and You alone we ask for help.
Had he known the interpretation of the beginning of the surah, that
Praise be to God, Lord of the Worlds
is a command from God to His servant
to say it, as we mentioned before of the report from Ibn ʿAbbās that Gabriel said to the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, from God: Say, O Muḥammad:
Praise be to God, Lord of the Worlds (2) Most Gracious, Most Merciful (3) Mālik of the Day of Judgement
You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help
, and had he understood from the Arabs that it is their habit, when they relate, or command the relating of, a report that follows saying, to address and then report [about an absent person]

, and to report about an absent person and then return to address, because relating by saying has the sense of both the absent and the addressed, as they say to a man: I said to your brother: If you stood, I would stand; and: I said to your brother: If he stood, I would stand, it would have become easy
for him to find the way out of what he found difficult to direct, the genitive
Mālik of the Day of Judgement
Mālik of the Day of Judgement
in the genitive, followed by a return to the address with
we mentioned before, is the well-known verse of Abū Kabīr al-Hudhalī
: Alas for my soul! the freshness
of Khālid, and the whiteness of your face, given to the dusty

earth! He returned to the address with his words “and the whiteness of your face” after the report about Khālid had been in the manner of a report about an absent person. And of this is the verse of Labīd b. Rabīʿa
spent the night complaining to me, about to weep

, when I have carried you seven years after seventy. He returned to addressing himself, after the report about it had preceded in the manner of a report about an absent person. And of this are the words of God, who is the most truthful in speech and the firmest proof:
Until, when you are in the ships and they sail with them with a good wind

So He addressed and then returned to reporting about the absent, and did not say: and they sail with you. The witnesses from verse and Arab speech for this are more than can be counted, and what we have mentioned suffices for one granted understanding of it. So the reading
(Mālika yawmi l-dīn) is forbidden and impermissible, because of the consensus of the authoritative body
of the reciters and scholars of the community on rejecting recitation by it.

evidence.text: Abū Jaʿfar said: The reciters differ in the recitation of {Mālik of the Day of Judgement}.
Some recite it (Malik of the Day of Judgement), some recite it {Mālik of the Day of Judgement}, and some recite it (Mālika yawmi l-dīn), with fatḥa on the kāf (4).

We have given an exhaustive account of the transmission from those from whom a reading on this has been reported, in the book “al-Qirāʾāt”, and informed of the reading we choose on it and the reason that makes what we chose of the reading sound; so we disliked repeating it in this place, since what we intend in this book of ours is the explanation of the interpretations of the verses of the Qurʾān, not of the modes of their recitation.

The interpretation of the reading of one who reads (Malik of the Day of Judgement) is that sovereignty belongs purely to God on the Day of Judgement, to the exclusion of all His creation who were before that in the world tyrant kings contending with Him for sovereignty and disputing His sole possession of pride, greatness, authority, and might; and so they became certain (1), by meeting God on the Day of Judgement, that they were the small and abased, and that to Him, apart (2) from them and from others, belong sovereignty, pride, might and splendour, as He, majestic is His mention and hallowed be His names, said in His revelation: {On the day when they come forth, nothing of them hidden from God: To whom belongs sovereignty this day? To God, the One, the Subduer} [Ghāfir 40:16].
As for the interpretation of the reading of one who reads {Mālik of the Day of Judgement}, it is what Abū Kurayb related to us:

Abū Jaʿfar said: Of the two interpretations, the more fitting for the verse, and of the two readings, the sounder in recitation in my view, is the first interpretation and (2) the reading of one who reads (Malik), in the sense of sovereignty; because in acknowledging His sole possession of sovereignty is a necessary affirmation of His sole possession of ownership, together with the excellence of the surplus of malik over mālik (3), since it is known that there is no king who is not an owner, while an owner may not be a king.

It is evident then that the sounder of the two readings and the more deserving of the two interpretations of the Book is the reading of one who reads (Malik of the Day of Judgement), in the sense of sovereignty belonging purely to Him on the Day of Judgement, rather than the reading of one who reads {Mālik of the Day of Judgement} in the sense (1) that He owns judgement between them and the decision of the verdict, alone in it among all His creation.
As for the interpretation of this in the reading of one who reads (Mālika yawmi l-dīn), he meant: O (5) Mālika of the Day of Judgement.

So the reading (1) (Mālika yawmi l-dīn) is forbidden and impermissible, because of the consensus of the authoritative body (2) of the reciters and scholars of the community on rejecting recitation by it.

x: The Discussion of the Interpretation of His words, majestic is His mention:
Dīn in this place has the sense of reckoning and recompense for deeds, as Kaʿb b. Juʿayl said
: If they shoot at us we shoot at them, and we repay them (dinnāhum) as they lend to us. And as another said
: [Know and be certain that your sovereignty will pass away]
, and know that as you requite (tadīnu), you will be requited (tudānu). He means: as you recompense, you will be recompensed. And of this are the words of God, majestic is His praise:
No indeed, but you deny the Dīn
and indeed there are over you guardians
[al-Infiṭār 82:9, 10], who record what you do of deeds. And His words, Exalted:
Then why, if you are not to be requited (madīnīn)

[al-Wāqiʿa 56:86], meaning not to be recompensed for your deeds nor reckoned with. Dīn has meanings in the speech of the Arabs other than the meaning of reckoning and recompense, which we shall mention in their places, God willing.
The reports from the early exegetes have come with what we said in the interpretation of His words
, with the witnesses confirming the interpretation they gave of it

c: Abū Kurayb Muḥammad b. al-ʿAlāʾ related to us: ʿUthmān b. Saʿīd told us: Bishr b. ʿUmāra told us: Abū Rawq told us, from al-Ḍaḥḥāk, from ʿAbd Allāh b.
m: . He said: The day of the reckoning of creatures, it is the Day of Resurrection; He requites them for their deeds, good for good and evil for evil, except for the one He pardons, for the command is His. Then He said:
Indeed, to Him belong creation and command

c: Mūsā b. Hārūn al-Hamdānī related to me: ʿAmr b. Ḥammād al-Qannād told us: Asbāṭ b. Naṣr al-Hamdānī told us, from Ismāʿīl b.
m: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Suddī, from Abū Mālik, and from Abū Ṣāliḥ, from Ibn ʿAbbās, and from Murra al-Hamdānī, from Ibn Masʿūd, and from some of the Companions of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace:
Mālik of the Day of Judgement
: it is the day of reckoning

c: Al-Ḥasan b. Yaḥyā related to us: ʿAbd al-Razzāq informed us: Maʿmar informed us, from Qatāda,
m: Mālik of the Day of Judgement
. He said: The day on which God requites His servants for their deeds

c: Al-Qāsim b. al-Ḥasan related to us: al-Ḥusayn b. Dāwūd told us: Ḥajjāj related to me, from Ibn Jurayj:
m: Mālik of the Day of Judgement
. He said: The day on which people are requited by reckoning.

x: The Discussion of the Interpretation of His words, Mighty and Majestic:
is: To You, O God, we humble ourselves, abase ourselves, and submit, in acknowledgement to You, our Lord, of lordship, and not to anyone other than You.

c: As Abū Kurayb related to us: ʿUthmān b. Saʿīd told us: Bishr b. ʿUmāra told us: Abū Rawq told us, from al-Ḍaḥḥāk, from ʿAbd Allāh b.
m: ʿAbbās, who said: Gabriel said to Muḥammad, may God bless him and grant him peace: Say, O Muḥammad:
: You alone we affirm as One, fear, and hope in, our Lord, and none other than You

. This saying of Ibn ʿAbbās has the same meaning as what we said. We chose to explain its interpretation as meaning: we humble ourselves, abase ourselves, and submit, rather than explaining it as meaning: we hope and fear, although hope and fear occur only with abasement; because servanthood (ʿubūdiyya) among all Arabs has abasement at its root, and they call the path that has been made smooth, which feet have trodden and travellers have rendered smooth, muʿabbad; of this is the verse of Ṭarafa b. al-ʿAbd
camels, and she sets one shank after another
on a trodden (muʿabbad) path (mawr). By mawr he means the path, and by muʿabbad the smoothed, trodden one

. From this the camel that has been made docile by being ridden on errands is called muʿabbad. And from this the servant (ʿabd) was called ʿabd because of his abasement to his master. The witnesses for this from the poetry of the Arabs and their speech are more than can be counted, and what we have mentioned suffices for one granted understanding of it, God Most High willing.

x: The Discussion of the Interpretation of His words:
and You alone we ask for help (5)
and You alone we ask for help
our Lord, we ask for help in our worship of You and our obedience

in all our affairs, and none other than You, since one who disbelieves in You asks for help in his affairs from the object of worship he worships among the idols besides You; whereas we ask You for help in all our affairs, devoting worship purely to You.

c: As Abū Kurayb related to us: ʿUthmān b. Saʿīd told us: Bishr b. ʿUmāra told us: Abū Rawq told us, from al-Ḍaḥḥāk, from ʿAbd Allāh b.
m: and You alone we ask for help
. He said: You alone we ask for help in obeying You and in all our affairs

x: What is the meaning of God's command to His servants that they ask Him for help in obeying Him? Is it permissible, when He has commanded them to obey Him, that He not help them in it? Or does anyone say to his Lord: “You alone we ask for help in obeying You” without being, by that saying, helped? And that is the obedience itself; so what is the point of the servant's asking his Lord for what He has already given

The interpretation of this is not the way you took. The believer who calls on his Lord to help him in obeying Him is calling for help during the remainder of his life in what He has charged him with of obedience, not for what has already passed of his righteous deeds in the earlier part of his life. And the servant's asking his Lord for this is permissible, because God's giving it to His servant, together with enabling his limbs to perform what He charged him with of obedience and made obligatory on him of obligations, is a favour from Him, majestic is His praise, with which He favoured him, and a kindness He showed him in it; and in His withholding favour from some of His servants in the matter of granting success, while the servant is occupied with disobeying Him and turning away from loving Him, and in His extending His favour to others, while the servant exerts himself in loving Him and hastens to obey Him, there is no corruption
in management and no injustice in judgement, such that an ignorant person might be ignorant of the place of God's ruling in His commanding
His servant to ask for His help in obeying Him. And in God's command, majestic is His praise, to His servants to say
You alone we worship and You alone we ask for help

, in the sense of their asking Him for help in worship, is the clearest proof of the falsity of the statement of those who hold tafwīḍ (delegation) among the Qadarīs, who held it impossible that God command any of His servants
with a command or charge him with an obligatory act, except after giving him help [and power]

to do it and to leave it. Were what they say in this so, the desire toward God for help in obeying Him would be void, since according to them, once command, prohibition and charge exist, it is a right incumbent on God toward the servant to give him help in it, whether his servant asks Him for it or leaves asking
for it; rather, according to them, His not giving that is an injustice from Him.
And if the matter were as they say, the one who says
You alone we worship and You alone we ask for help

would only be asking his Lord not to act unjustly. And in the consensus of all the people of Islam that the saying of one who says “O God, we ask You for help” is right, and their declaring wrong the saying of one who says “O God, do not wrong us”, is a clear proof of the error of what those whose view I described said, since the interpretation, according to them, of the saying “O God, we ask You for help” is: O God, do not leave off our help, whose leaving off
would be an injustice from You.
You alone we worship and You alone we ask for help
, so that the report of worship was put first and the request for help in it put after it
, when worship occurs only with help, so the request for help was more deserving of being put first
, before the action for which help is sought
and the worship done by it?

Since it was known that the servant has no way to worship except with help from God, majestic is His praise, and it was impossible for the servant to be a worshipper unless he is helped in worship, and for him to be helped in it unless he does it, the placing first of whichever of the two was placed before its companion is equivalent, just as it is the same whether you say to a man

who has done your need and done well by you in doing it: “You fulfilled my need and were kind to me,” putting first the mention of his fulfilling your need, or you say: “You were kind to me and fulfilled my need,” putting the mention of kindness before the mention of fulfilling the need; because he is not one who fulfils your need unless he is kind to you, nor kind to you unless he fulfils your need. Likewise it is the same whether the speaker says: O God, You alone we worship, so help us in worshipping You; or says: O God, help us in worshipping You, for You alone we worship.
Some of the heedless have supposed that this belongs to the advanced that has the sense of being postponed, as Imruʾ al-Qays said

: Had what I strive for been for a modest livelihood, a little of wealth would have sufficed me, and I would not have sought. He means: a little wealth would have sufficed me, and I would not have sought much. That is among the meanings of advancing and postponing, and it is far from resembling the verse of Imruʾ al-Qays, because a little wealth may suffice a man while he still seeks much, so the finding of what suffices him of it does not oblige him to give up seeking much, and so it would be the like of worship, where the existence of worship brings the existence of help for it, and the existence of help for it brings its existence, so that mention of one of them indicates the other, and the placing first of whichever is placed before its companion is equivalent in soundness of speech, each being set in its own rank and placed in its own position.
If he says: What is the reason for repeating
, when it had already come before
? Why was it not said: You alone we worship and ask for help, since the one reported as worshipped is the one reported as the one asked for help? It is said to him
: The kāf that is with iyyā is the kāf that would have attached to the verb, I mean His words
, had it been placed after the verb
; it is the pronoun of the addressed person in the accusative with the verb, and it was multiplied by iyyā when put first
, since nouns, when they stand alone, are not in the speech of the Arabs on a single letter. Since the kāf in

is the pronoun of the addressed, which would be a kāf alone attached to the verb if it came after the verb, and since its due is to be repeated with every verb it attaches to, so that one says: O God, we worship You, ask You for help, praise You, and thank You, and that is more eloquent in the speech of the Arabs than saying: O God, we worship You and ask for help and praise, so likewise, when

the pronoun of the addressed is put before the verb, connected with iyyā, the more eloquent course is to repeat it with every verb, just as the eloquent course in speech was to repeat it with every verb when it came after the verb attached to it, although leaving off its repetition is permissible.
Some who did not examine closely
have supposed that the repetition of
, after its precedence in His words
, is like the verse of ʿAdī b. Zayd al-ʿIbādī
with no concealment in it, between the day and between the night, which have been set apart And like the verse of Aʿshā of Hamdān
: Between al-Ashajj and between Qays is a towering eminence
and for the one born. And that, on the part of its sayer, is ignorance, because the due of

is to be repeated with every verb, for the reason we described above, and that is not the ruling of “between” (bayna), because “between,” when it requires two, is found only repeated if it is repeated, since it does not stand alone with one, and because if it were made to stand alone with one of the two nouns while requiring two, the speech would be as if impossible.
For if a speaker were to say
: The sun has divided between the day, it would be defective speech

, because the speech falls short of what it needs for the completion that “between” requires. But if the speaker were to say: O God, You alone we worship, that would be complete speech. So it was known by that that the need of every phrase that is the like of
for “iyyāka” is like the need of
for it, and that the right course is for “iyyāka” to be with it

, since each phrase of them is a complete predicate clause of a subject; and it is evident that this differs in ruling from the ruling of “between” in that in which the one whose statement we described tried to align the two.
The Discussion of the Interpretation of His words:
Guide us to the straight path
in this place, in our view, is: grant us success in remaining steadfast in it. As it has been reported

c: Abū Kurayb related to us: ʿUthmān b. Saʿīd told us: Bishr b. ʿUmāra told us: Abū Rawq told us, from al-Ḍaḥḥāk, from ʿAbd Allāh b.
m: ʿAbbās, who said: Gabriel said to Muḥammad: Say, O Muḥammad:
Guide us to the straight path
: Inspire us with the guiding way
. And His inspiring him with that is His granting him success, as we have said in its interpretation. Its meaning is like the meaning of His words
and You alone we ask for help

, in that it is the servant's petition to his Lord for success in remaining steadfast in acting in obedience to Him, and in hitting upon the truth and the right in what He commanded him and forbade him, in what lies ahead of his lifetime, not what has already passed of his deeds and been concluded in what is past of his life, just as His words
and You alone we ask for help

are a petition from him to his Lord for help in performing what He has charged him with of obedience in the remainder of his lifetime. So the meaning of the speech is: O God, You alone we worship, alone, with no partner for You, devoting worship to You exclusively, to the exclusion of any other gods and idols; so help us in Your worship, and grant us success in what You granted success to those You have favoured among Your prophets and the people of obedience to You, of the paths

x: If someone says: And where did you find hidāya in the speech of the Arabs with the meaning of tawfīq (granting success)? [It is said to him]
: That is in their speech more frequent and more manifest than that the number of attestations that have come from them for it could be counted; of this is the verse of the poet
: Do not deny me — may God guide you — my request, and let me not be like one whom travel has destroyed meaning
: may God grant you success in fulfilling my need. And of this is the verse of another

— may the King guide you — for every occasion has its fitting word. So it is known that he only meant: may God grant you success in hitting upon the truth in my affair. And of this are the words of God, Mighty and Majestic:
and God does not guide the wrongdoing people

And it is known by that that He did not mean that He does not make clear to the wrongdoers what is obligatory on them of His obligations. And how could that be its meaning, when He has covered with explanation all those under obligation among His creatures? Rather, He, exalted be His mention, meant that He does not grant them success and does not open their breasts to the truth and to faith. And some of them have claimed that the interpretation of His words

is: increase us in guidance. This statement cannot be free of one of two things: either its sayer supposed that the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, was commanded [to petition his Lord for]
an increase in help and success. If he supposed that he was commanded to petition

for an increase in explanation, that has no ground, because God, majestic is His praise, does not charge a servant with any of His obligations except after making it clear to him and establishing the proof against him by it; and if the meaning of that were the meaning of petitioning for explanation, he would have been commanded to call upon his Lord to make clear to him what He had made obligatory on him, and that in supplication is defective, because He does not impose an obligation except made clear to the one on whom He imposes it; or else he was commanded to call upon his Lord to impose on him the obligations that He had not imposed.
And in the invalidity of this line of the servant's petition to his Lord there is what makes plain that the meaning of
Guide us to the straight path

is other than: make clear to us Your obligations and Your limits. Or else he supposed that he was commanded to petition his Lord for an increase in help and success; if that is so, then his petition for that increase cannot be free of being a petition for an increase of help with regard to what has already passed of his deeds, or with regard to what will occur; and in the removal of the servant's need for help with regard to what has been concluded of his deeds there is what shows that the meaning of the petition for that increase is only his petition for an increase for what will occur of his deeds. And since that is so, the matter comes back to what we described and said on this, that it is the servant's petition to his Lord for success in performing what he is charged with of [his Lord's obligations]
in what lies ahead of his lifetime.
And in the soundness of that is the refutation of the statement

of the people of qadar [the Qadariyya], who claim that everyone commanded with a command or charged with an obligation has been given of help for it that which removes, as to that obligation, his need of his Lord; for if the matter were as they say, the meaning of God's words, majestic is His praise:
You alone we worship and You alone we ask for help (5) Guide us to the straight path
would be void. And in the soundness of its meaning as we have explained lies the refutation of their statement. And some of them have claimed that the meaning of His words
Guide us to the straight path

then guide them to the path of Hell

and You alone we ask for help
