x: There has been disagreement about the description of wrath on the part of God, exalted be His mention.

Some of them said: God's wrath against any of His creatures with whom He is angry is the bringing down of His punishment on the one with whom He is angry, whether in his worldly life or in his hereafter, as He described Himself, exalted be His mention, in His Book, saying:
So when they angered Us, We took vengeance on them and drowned them all
Say: Shall I inform you of something worse than that as to recompense with God? Those whom God has cursed and with whom He is angry, and of whom He made apes and swine

[al-Māʾida 5:60]. And some of them said: God's wrath against any of His servants with whom He is angry is His censure of them and of their deeds, and His reviling of them in speech. And some of them said: Wrath on His part is an understood meaning, like what is known of the meanings of wrath, except that — although it is so in respect of affirmation — its meaning on His part differs from the meaning of the wrath of human beings, which disturbs them, stirs them, burdens them and harms them; because God, majestic is His praise, is not subject in His essence to afflictions, but it is an attribute of His, as knowledge is an attribute of His, and power is an attribute of His, as is understood in respect of affirmation, even though the meanings of those differ from the meanings of the knowledge of servants, which are cognitions of hearts, and their faculties, which exist with the existence of acts and cease with their ceasing

evidence.text: Abū Jaʿfar said: The reciters are unanimous in reading {ghayr} with a kasra on the rāʾ.

And it is also permissible to put {ghayr} in the accusative (2) in {ghayr al-maghḍūbi ʿalayhim}, although I dislike the reading of it so, for its irregularity (shudhūdh) from the reading of the reciters, and because whatever departs, of readings, from what the community has brought by manifest, widespread transmission is an opinion contrary to the truth, and one deviating from the way of God and the way of His Messenger, may God bless him and grant him peace, and the way of the Muslims, even if it has — [were the reading of it permissible] (3) — a way out in soundness.

And one of the Basran grammarians used to claim that the reading of whoever put ghayr in the accusative in {ghayr al-maghḍūbi ʿalayhim} is on the aspect of an exception: {ghayr al-maghḍūbi ʿalayhim} excepted from the meanings of the description of {alladhīna anʿamta ʿalayhim}, as if he thought that the meaning of those who read it in the accusative is: Guide us to the straight path, the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour, except those upon whom wrath has been brought, who are those You have not favoured in their religions and have not guided to the truth, so do not make us among them.

And the correct view on its interpretation and reading, in our opinion, is the first view, which is the reading of {ghayr al-maghḍūbi ʿalayhim} with a kasra on the rāʾ of {ghayr}, on the interpretation that it is an attribute of {alladhīna anʿamta ʿalayhim} and a qualifier of them — for what we have set out already — if you wish; and if you wish, on the interpretation of repeating {ṣirāṭa}; all of that is correct and good.

nor of those who go astray (7)
One of the people of Basra
was inserted to complete the speech, and that its meaning is its nullification
, and he cites in support of his statement [the verse of]

: In a well of no ḥūr he went by night, and did not perceive and he interprets it as: in a well of ḥūr he went by night; that is: in a well of ruin; and that “lā” has the sense of nullification and a filler particle (ṣila)

— and he means: I do not blame the fair ones for mocking. And with the verse of al-Aḥwaṣ
for pleasure that I not love it … while pleasure has a persistent caller, not heedless.
He means: they blame me for pleasure that I love it. And with His, exalted, words:
What prevented you that you did not prostrate
[al-Aʿrāf 7:12]. He means: that you prostrate. And it is related of the sayer of this statement that he used to interpret

as having the sense of “siwā” (other than). So the meaning of the speech in his view would be: Guide us to the straight path, the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour, who are other than those who incur wrath and
those who go astray. And one of the Kufan grammarians
used to reject this of his statement, and claimed that if

had the sense of “siwā”, it would be an error to coordinate on it with “lā”, since “lā” is coordinated with only on a negation that has preceded it, just as it would be an error for a speaker to say: I have siwā your brother and not your father.
Because “siwā” is not among the particles of negation and denial.
Since that is an error in the speech of the Arabs, and the Qurʾān is in the most eloquent
of the languages of the Arabs, it was known that what the sayer claimed — that
means: other than those who incur wrath — is an error, since he then reverted the speech upon it with “lā”, and claimed that
there has only the sense of denial, and

it was sound in the speech of the Arabs and widespread and manifest in their discourse to direct “ghayr” to the sense of negation, and it is used among them: Your brother is ghayr a doer of good and not a doer of beauty.

By that is meant: Your brother is neither a doer of good nor a doer of beauty. And he rejects that “lā” should come with the sense of deletion in speech at the beginning of it, when no negation has preceded it. And he says: If its coming with the sense of deletion at the beginning were permissible, before an indication pointing to that in the form of a preceding negation, the statement of one who said would be sound: I wanted not to honour your brother — meaning: I wanted to honour your brother. And he used to say: In the testimony of the people of knowledge of the tongue of the Arabs to the error of the sayer of that there is clear indication that “lā” does not come at the beginning with the sense of deletion when no negation has preceded it. And he used to interpret the “lā” in the verse of al-ʿAjjāj, which
we mentioned that the Basran cited in support of his statement

, as a genuine negation, and that the meaning of the verse is: He went by night in a well that does not yield him any good, and no trace of work is evident to him in it, and he does not perceive that, nor know

From their saying: The grinder ground and did not yield anything (mā aḥārat shayʾan). That is: no trace of work was evident to it. And he says of the other verses, I mean like the verse of Abū al-Najm: So I do not blame the fair ones for not mocking it was permissible for “lā” to have the sense of deletion only because negation had preceded it at the beginning of the speech, so the latter speech was connected with the first, as the poet said
: The Messenger of God would not have been pleased with their deed … nor the two good ones, Abū Bakr and (lā) ʿUmar. That was permissible because negation had preceded at the start of the speech.

And this other view is more likely to be correct than the first, since it is not found in the speech of the Arabs to begin speech, without a preceding negation, with “lā” whose meaning is deletion, nor is coordination with it on “siwā” permissible, nor on a particle of exception. And “ghayr” in the speech of the Arabs has only three meanings: one is exception, another negation, and the third siwā. So when [it is established that it is an error for “lā” to be]
in the sense of nullification at the beginning, and it is invalid for it to be coordinated on

were it in the sense of “illā”, which is exception, and it is also not permissible for it to be coordinated on it were it in the sense of “siwā”, with “lā” present as coordinated by the wāw that coordinates it on what is before it — it is sound and established that there is no aspect of
to which it may soundly be directed except the sense of negation and denial, and that there is no aspect to His words

So the interpretation of the speech then — since what we have said is sound by what we have cited as evidence — is: Guide us to the straight path, the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour, not
those who incur wrath and not those who go astray.
And who are these ones who go astray, from whose way and from whose error God commanded us to seek refuge in God, lest He make us travel their way and
They are those whom God described in His revelation, saying:

O People of the Book, do not exceed the bounds in your religion other than the truth, and do not follow the whims of a people who went astray before, and led many astray, and strayed from the right way
And what is your proof that these are they?

x: from the straight course and travels other than the upright way is “astray” (ḍāll) among the Arabs, because of his losing the direction of the road; for that reason God, exalted be His mention, named the Christians “those who go astray,” for their error regarding the truth, the course of the way, and their taking of religion in other than the straight path.
Is not that too a description of the Jews?
Then how did He single out the Christians with this description, and single out the Jews with what He described them with, that they are those who incur wrath?

Both groups are astray and have incurred wrath; but God, majestic is His praise, marked each group of them, in His describing to His servants, with what they know it by when He mentions it to them or informs them of it, and did not name either of the two groups except with what is a description of it in truth, even if it has additions to it of attributes of blame. [And] some of the people of dullness among the Qadariyya [have supposed]
that in God's, majestic is His praise, describing the Christians as astray in His words
and His ascribing the going astray to them rather than ascribing their being led astray to Himself, and His leaving off describing them as being led astray (al-muḍallalūn)

, as He described the Jews as those who incur wrath, is evidence for the soundness of what his brethren among the ignorant Qadariyya said — out of his ignorance of the breadth of the speech of the Arabs and the varieties of its aspects. Had the matter been as the dullard whose case we have described supposed, it would be necessary that the case

of everything described by an attribute, or to which an act is ascribed, be such that it is impermissible for there to be in it a cause for another, and that everything in which there is [of that, for another,]

a cause, the truth about it is that it be ascribed to its causer; and were that necessary, it would be an error to say: The tree moved, when the winds moved it; and the earth shook, when the earthquake shook it, and the like of this kind of speech that would make a book long to enumerate.
And in the words of God, majestic is His praise:
until when you are in the ships and they run with them

the running to the ships, although their running is by another's making them run, there is that which indicates the error of the interpretation of the one whose statement we have described regarding His words
, and his claim that in God's, majestic is His praise, attributing going astray to those of the Christians to whom He attributed it, there is a validation of what the deniers claimed, that
God has in the acts of His creatures a cause

on account of which their acts came to exist, notwithstanding God's, majestic is His praise, making plain in express terms in many verses of His revelation that He is the one who leads astray and guides; of this are His words, Mighty and Majestic:

Have you seen him who takes his desire as his god, and God has led him astray knowingly, and sealed his hearing and his heart, and placed over his sight a veil. Who then will guide him after God? Will you not remember?

So He, majestic is His praise, announced that He is the one who leads astray and guides, and no other. But the Qurʾān was revealed in the tongue of the Arabs, as we have already explained at the beginning of the book, and it is the way of the Arabs sometimes to ascribe the act to the one from whom it came into being, even if its causer is other than the one from whom it came into being, and sometimes to its causer, even if the one from whom the act came into being is other; so how about the act that the servant acquires by acquisition (kasb), and that God, majestic is His praise, brings into existence in its essence [and its coming-to-be]

! Rather, that is more fitting to be ascribed to the one who acquires it as an acquisition of his, by the power he has over it and the choice he has for it, and to God, majestic is His praise, by the bringing into existence of its essence
A question that the people of heresy who attack the Qurʾān ask, if one of them asks us, saying: You have stated

at the beginning of this book of yours, in describing explanation (bayān), that its highest in rank and noblest in station is that which is most eloquent in making clear the need of the one making clear by it on his own behalf, plainest as to the intent of its sayer, and nearest to the understanding of its hearer; and you said besides that the most fitting of speech to be so is the speech of God, majestic is His praise, because of its excellence

, by the elevation of its rank above the highest ranks of explanation; so what is the reason — if the matter is as you have described — for the lengthening of speech in the like of Sūrat Umm al-Qurʾān with seven verses, when two of them have already contained the meanings of all of them, namely His words: (Malik of the Day of Judgement * You alone we worship and You alone we ask for help).

For there is no doubt that whoever knows the King (malik) of the Day of Judgement has known Him by His most beautiful names and His loftiest attributes, and that whoever is obedient to God is undoubtedly a follower of the way of those upon whom God has bestowed favour in their religion, and one who turns away from the way of those with whom He is angry and who have gone astray; so what is there in the addition of the remaining five verses of wisdom that the two verses we mentioned did not contain? It is said to him: God, exalted be His mention, gathered for our Prophet Muḥammad, may God bless him and grant him peace, and for his community, by what He sent down to him of His Book, meanings that He did not gather in a book

He sent down to a prophet before him, nor for any of the nations before them; for every book that He, exalted be His mention, sent down on one of His prophets before him, He sent down with only some of the meanings that the entirety of His Book that He sent down to our Prophet Muḥammad contains, such as the Torah, which is admonitions and detailed exposition, the Psalms, which is praise and glorification, and the Gospel, which is admonitions and reminding, none of them having a miracle that testifies in confirmation of the one to whom it was sent down; while the Book that was sent down on our Prophet Muḥammad, may God bless him and grant him peace, contains the meanings of all of that and adds to it many meanings of which all the other books are empty, and we have already mentioned them earlier in this book
And among the noblest of those meanings by which our Book excels all books before it are its wondrous composition (naẓm), its strange arrangement (raṣf)
, and its marvellous structure, such that orators were unable to compose the like of its smallest sūra, and the eloquent were too weary to arrange the like of part

of it, and poets were bewildered at its structure and the understandings of the intelligent were dulled before it, falling short of bringing the like of it, so they found for it nothing but submission and acknowledgement that it is from the One, the Subduer; along with what it contains in addition of meanings that are encouragement and warning, command and prohibition, narratives, disputation and parable, and the like of those meanings that have not been gathered

in any book sent down to earth from heaven. So whatever lengthiness it has of the sort found in Umm al-Qurʾān, it is for what I described before: that God, exalted be His mention, wished to combine, by its wondrous arrangement and strange composition, which departs from the metres of poems, the rhymed prose of soothsayers, the speeches of orators and the letters of the eloquent, the like of which all humankind are unable to arrange and the equal of which all servants are unable to compose — the indication of the prophethood of our Prophet Muḥammad, may God bless him and grant him peace.

And by what it contains of praise, glorification and laudation of Him, to alert servants to His greatness, authority, power and the vastness of His kingdom, so that they remember Him by His blessings, praise Him for His favours, thereby deserve more from Him and earn from Him abundant reward. And by what it contains of the description of those whom He has favoured with knowledge of Him and graced with success in obeying Him, to teach His servants that every blessing they have in their religion and worldly life is from Him, so that they direct their desire to Him and seek their needs from Him rather than from other gods and equals. And by what it contains of mention of the exemplary punishments He inflicted on those who disobeyed Him and the penalties He sent down on those who opposed His command, to make servants fearful of committing disobedience to Him and of exposing themselves to what they have no strength to bear of His anger, lest the way of those of the destroyed who committed it be followed with them in chastisement and retribution.
That, then, is the reason for lengthening the explanation in Sūrat Umm al-Qurʾān, and in what is its like of the other sūras of the Furqān, and that is the far-reaching wisdom and the perfect proof.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmitted it in his Tafsīr 1/26 (9) via Muḥammad b. al-ʿAlāʾ with this chain.

Sharḥ his Dīwān p. 352, and Lisān al-ʿArab (j-h-sh). Ibn Sallām said in Ṭabaqāt fuḥūl al-shuʿarāʾ 1/61, having mentioned the verse: There is no disagreement that this is forged, with which reports multiply ……

Waqʿat Ṣiffīn p. 57, al-Kāmil 1/327, and al-Mukhaṣṣaṣ 17/155 (vol. 5).

al-waẓīf: from the camel's fetlock to its knee in the forelegs, and in the hind legs from the fetlock to the hock. Lisān al-ʿArab (w-ẓ-f).

Dīwān of al-Ḥuṭayʾa p. 222, al-Aghānī 2/187, Lisān (q-w-l), (ḥ-n-n); in al-Fākhir p. 314 it is said that the first to say it was Ṭarafa b. al-ʿAbd, in a poem in which he apologises to ʿAmr b. Hind. We did not find the verse in his Dīwān.

Its chain is very weak; Abū al-Mukhtār al-Ṭāʾī and the nephew of al-Ḥārith are unknown, and al-Ḥārith is weak. It was transmitted by Ibn Abī Shayba 10/482, al-Dārimī 2/435, al-Tirmidhī (2906), al-Bayhaqī in al-Shuʿab (1935, 1936), and al-Baghawī in his Tafsīr 1/39 and in Sharḥ al-sunna (1181), by way of Ḥusayn with it, at length. It was also transmitted by Isḥāq b. Rāhawayh in his Musnad — as in al-Nukat al-ẓirāf 7/357 — Ibn Naṣr in Qiyām al-layl p. 71, Ibn Abī Ḥātim in his Tafsīr 1/30 (32) — abridged — al-Bazzār (836) — at length — and al-Dāraquṭnī in al-ʿIlal 3/141, 142, by several routes from Ḥamza al-Zayyāt with it. There was disagreement about Ḥamza al-Zayyāt concerning it, and the sound version is the one the author cited. See ʿIlal al-Dāraquṭnī 3/138–140. Al-Dhahabī said in the entry for Abū al-Mukhtār in al-Mīzān 4/571: His hadith on the merits of the noble Qurʾān is munkar. And Ibn Kathīr said in Faḍāʾil al-Qurʾān p. 15: The hadith is well known from the transmission of al-Ḥārith al-Aʿwar, and they have spoken against him — indeed some have called him a liar on account of his opinion and belief; as for his deliberately lying in hadith, no, and God knows best. The most that can be said of this hadith is that it is the speech of the Commander of the Faithful ʿAlī, may God be pleased with him, and some erred in raising it to the Prophet, and it is good, sound speech. And he said in his Tafsīr 1/42: It has also been reported as mawqūf from ʿAlī, and that is likelier. It is reported by another route, abridged, in Aḥmad 2/111 (704), and it does not contain the interpretation of the straight path.
Al-Khaṭīb transmitted it in al-Faqīh wa-l-mutafaqqih (190) by way of Ismāʿīl with it. And al-Bazzār (835) — abridged — =

= and al-Dārimī 2/435, 436 by way of Muḥammad b. Salama with it. Al-Khaṭīb (191) transmitted it by way of Muḥammad b. Ḥumayd, from al-Ḥakam b. Bashīr b. Salmān, from ʿAmr b. Qays, from ʿAmr b. Murra with it. Abū Sinān is truthful (ṣadūq) with some errors, and he was contradicted in it, for more than one transmitted it from ʿAmr b. Murra, from Abū al-Bakhtarī, from Ibn Abī al-Ḥārith, from al-Ḥārith, from ʿAlī. See ʿIlal al-Dāraquṭnī 3/137, 138.
